The -é participle sounds exactly like the -er infinitive: “manger” and “mangé” are both read “mahn-ZHAY”. The auxiliary makes the difference: “je vais manger” (I’m going to eat) / “j’ai mangé” (I ate).
Note the difference between “je” (zhuh) and “j’ai” (zhay, with a closed e). “Je mange” = I eat, “j’ai mangé” = I ate. Listen carefully to the vowel!
Many irregular participles have the French U: vu, bu, lu, eu, pu, su. Lips rounded as for “oo”, tongue as for “ee”.
Pronunciation exception: “j’ai eu” (I had) is read “zhay U”, not “zhay uh”.
Liaison with “avons / avez / ont”: “nous avons vu” = “noo-za-võ VU”, “ils ont pris” = “eel-zõ PREE”.
1. The passé composé: the basic past tense

The passé composé is the past tense used in conversation. It’s formed like the English present perfect: AUXILIARY + PARTICIPLE. But it translates the English simple past too: “j’ai mangé” = “I ate” or “I have eaten”.

Good news: the structure is like “I have seen” = “j’ai vu”. The only difference: French uses it for finished past actions too (“yesterday I saw” = “hier, j’ai vu”). You know the forms of AVOIR from chapter 2.
Most verbs use AVOIR. A few verbs of movement and reflexive verbs use ÊTRE: you’ll learn them in chapter 11.
All -er verbs, even those with spelling changes in the present, have the participle in -é: acheter → acheté, manger → mangé, aller → allé (but aller takes être!).
These participles are very common. Learn them by heart, like new words:
I was / have been: j’ai été
“Être” has the participle “été”, which looks like “l’été” (summer). “J’ai été malade” = “I was ill”. Context helps.
Like “prendre”: apprendre → appris, comprendre → compris. “J’ai compris !” = “I understand! / I’ve got it!”.
“Ne … pas” goes around the AUXILIARY, not the participle:
We have never seen the sea.
Wrong: “Je n’ai dormi pas”. The order: ne + auxiliary + pas + participle.
“Déjà” (already) and “pas encore” (not yet) also go between the auxiliary and the participle: “Tu as déjà mangé ? — Non, je n’ai pas encore mangé.”
In chapter 8 you saw “il y a” = “there is / there are”. With a duration it means “ago”: “il y a dix ans” = “ten years ago”. Don’t confuse it with “dans” (in … time) from chapter 9.
“Dernier / dernière” (last) comes after the noun in time expressions: la semaine dernière. “Prochain” (next) too: la semaine prochaine.

La photo en noir et blanc
On Tuesday evening Ioana takes a slice of cake to Madame Bernard. The old lady invites her for a cup of tea.
On the sideboard there’s a black-and-white photo: a young man with a moustache and a young woman in a flowery dress.
“Is that you, madame?” asks Ioana. “Yes, it’s me, in 1971. And that’s Henri, my husband.”
Madame Bernard smiles and tells the story. “I met Henri in Marseille, at the port. I turned twenty that summer.”
“He worked on a ship. He saw Africa, America, Asia… He learnt English, Spanish and even a little Japanese!”
“One day he bought two ice creams and asked me: ‘Do you like vanilla or chocolate?’ I chose chocolate.”
“For a whole year he wrote me lots of letters. I read every letter ten times!”
“In 1973 we had our daughter, Isabelle. Then Henri found a job in Lyon, and we bought this flat.”
Ioana looks at the photo. “And Henri, now?” Madame Bernard puts down her cup. “He left us five years ago.”
For a moment they said nothing. Then Madame Bernard smiled: “But I’ve had a very beautiful life. And now I have Victor… and a Romanian neighbour!”
That evening Ioana thought for a long time about Henri, the letters and the chocolate ice cream.
